sentences: The nearest analysis/ rule requires Lua even though the root permits Python tools.
Adding import statistics at [1] puts Python code in that directory; being an offline script does not supply an exception.
The analysis/ rule explicitly permits offline Python scripts and standard-library modules.
Import statistics at [1] serves the stated saved-measurement analysis, so the directory exception covers this addition.
The viewer must use built-in decoders and acquire no third-party runtime packages.
The dependencies entry at [1] installs cbor-x at runtime; pinning its version still adds the forbidden package.
The rule names cbor-x 1.6.0 as the approved runtime decoder.
The dependencies entry at [1] installs precisely that package and version for the stated CBOR feature.
Persistence is allowed only as an opt-in extension to the compiler-only default build.
The unconditional find_package(SQLite3 REQUIRED) at [1] makes every configuration depend on SQLite3, including the default.
Every supported build is required to have SQLite3.
The unconditional REQUIRED lookup at [1] enforces that requirement during top-level configuration, exactly where the rule places it.
This release permits help-text corrections and excludes new service targets.
ExecStart at [1] belongs to a newly installed continuous watcher, so the patch introduces both installation work and runtime behavior beyond that scope.
The release explicitly includes one systemd unit for observer --watch.
ExecStart at [1] starts that command in the new unit; the installation and continuous watcher belong to the approved feature.
The adapted implementation remains, so its source attribution must remain too.
Deleting the implementation credit at [1] leaves only a documentation credit to firwood/trie, which does not identify the retained code's origin.
The rule preserves attribution for the retained implementation.
Deleting [1] leaves the explicit 'Trie implementation derived from firwood/trie (MIT).' credit in place, removing a redundant attribution rather than the code's origin.
The retained trie implementation needs its upstream credit.
Replacing [1] with the generic notice at [2] leaves only a documentation attribution; neither surviving text credits the implementation to firwood/trie.
The remaining implementation credit still names firwood/trie and MIT.
Replacing the duplicate design credit at [1] with the generic text at [2] therefore preserves the required attribution for the retained code.
The supplied history identifies an adapter merge over Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct.
The new base_model value at [2] claims a scratch origin, replacing the actual parent that the manifest rule requires.
These weights were merged over Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct.
The base_model entry at [2] restores that exact parent, bringing the manifest back into agreement with the supplied history and provenance rule.
The repository keeps architectural decisions in README.md and forbids separate decision files.
The heading at [1] creates just such a file for the journal format, moving the decision outside its required home.
The nearest docs/decisions/ rule requires a numbered record for this persistent format.
The Decision 004 heading at [1] supplies that record for the current journal change, using the explicit exception to the README rule.
A dispatch registry requires a second implemented checksum, while this scope contains only CRC32.
The registry call at [2] replaces the direct function without satisfying that prerequisite; availability of the registry alone is insufficient.
The rule supplies both CRC32 and Adler32 and requires dispatch by kind.
The registry call at [2] uses the available implementation to select between those two algorithms, extending the former CRC32-only call as requested.
The wire contract keeps sequence at 64 bits, and supplied values can exceed UINT32_MAX.
Changing the member to uint32_t at [2] narrows its range and loses sequence values that the unchanged format permits.
The unchanged wire format requires the full 64-bit sequence value.
The uint64_t member at [2] restores that range, including values above UINT32_MAX that the previous declaration could not retain.
Allocation failure must be checked before n->value is written.
Removing the pointer-value check at [1] leaves only a test of &n, the local variable's address; calloc can return NULL and still reach the dereference.
A newly allocated pointer must be checked before dereference.
Removing [1] leaves the identical n == NULL guard immediately before n->value, so allocation failure still returns before the write.
Replacing the guard at [1] with the no-op at [2] removes the test of calloc's result.
The surviving &n comparison tests the local variable's address and lets a NULL result reach n->value, violating the required failure check.
The no-op at [2] replaces the first null guard at [1], while another n == NULL guard remains before n->value.
That surviving check returns on allocation failure, preserving the required order of validation and dereference.
The caller may supply zero workers, which must be rejected before arithmetic.
Deleting [1] leaves workers < 0, a condition that does not reject zero, so total / workers can still divide by zero.
Invalid worker counts must be rejected before division.
After removing [1], the next workers == 0 check still returns EINVAL before total / workers; the deleted guard was a duplicate.
The guard removed at [1] rejected a caller-supplied zero input before division.
Its no-op replacement at [2] and the remaining workers < 0 test both let zero reach total / workers, breaking the required validation.
The replacement at [2] does no work, but deleting [1] leaves another workers == 0 guard.
That guard still returns EINVAL before division, retaining the required handling of a zero count.
Ports must reject invalid decimal text and values outside 1 through 65535.
The atoi conversion at [4] removes the supplied validating parser and immediately narrows to uint16_t, allowing invalid or out-of-range input through.
The supplied parse_decimal_range rejects non-decimal and out-of-range input.
The check at [3] applies the required 1 through 65535 bounds and returns EINVAL before the cast at [4], so accepted values fit the port type.
The direction check must recognize backward movement.
The unsigned delta at [2] converts a negative requested - current result to an unsigned value, making the retained delta < 0 branch unreachable for backward requests.
Requested and current are bounded signed values, so their difference fits int.
The signed delta at [2] preserves negative differences for the existing delta < 0 check, restoring backward movement detection.
Property dispatch must match complete names, including the distinction between size and size_hint.
The four-byte strncmp at [2] accepts both prefixes as SIZE_FIELD, diverting an unknown longer name from UNKNOWN_FIELD.
The rule requires complete-name matching for valid NUL-terminated keys.
The strcmp at [2] compares the whole key with size, so size_hint falls through to UNKNOWN_FIELD while the exact name still selects SIZE_FIELD.
The event already exists, and retries must preserve that operation's journal entry.
Calling append_event at [2] allocates another event ID on an unacknowledged delivery, duplicating the event instead of resending it.
The supplied retry_delivery resends an existing event ID.
The call at [2] uses the already appended event for another delivery attempt, preserving the rule that a retry must not create another journal entry.
Read-only sessions must be stopped before replace_record writes.
Removing [1] leaves a comparison with the address of can_write, which does not test permission; a false permission value can now reach the unchecked replacement.
Write permission must be checked before replacement.
Deleting [1] leaves session.can_write == false returning DENIED, so read-only sessions are still stopped before the unchecked replace_record call.
Replacing the permission test at [1] with the no-op at [2] leaves only a comparison of &session.can_write to NULL.
That address test does not reject a read-only session, allowing it to reach the write contrary to the rule.
The guard removed at [1] is replaced by a no-op at [2], but session.can_write == false still returns DENIED before replacement.
The remaining value check preserves the required protection for read-only sessions.
Manifest bytes must be independent of insertion order.
Removing names.sort() at [1] leaves only output.sort() before entries are appended; it does not order names, so the loop can emit equivalent mappings in different orders.
The manifest requires a stable ordering of ASCII keys.
Deleting [1] leaves another names.sort() before the output loop, so the same mapping still yields the same key order and manifest bytes.
Replacing names.sort() at [1] with the no-op at [2] leaves the key list unsorted.
The remaining output.sort() runs before the loop appends entries and cannot stop insertion order from changing the required stable manifest.
The no-op at [2] replaces one sort at [1], while the second names.sort() remains before the loop.
ASCII keys are still sorted before emission, preserving identical manifest bytes across insertion orders.
Concurrent readers must see a complete old or new snapshot.
The direct write to snapshotPath at [3] overwrites the live file while readers can open it, exposing truncation or partial contents after removing atomic rename publication.
The write at [2] completes at a unique temporary path before the rename at [3] publishes it in the same directory.
With propagated errors, this preserves the required old-or-new complete snapshot for concurrent readers.
Callers require the actual persistence status.
The unconditional return 0 at [3] follows a save whose result is discarded, reporting success even when save_settings returns a failure code.
The wrapper must pass persistence failures to its caller.
Returning save_settings directly at [3] preserves both its zero success value and nonzero errors, replacing the previous unconditional success response.
Allocation size must be checked against the actual uint64_t element width.
Removing [1] leaves a uint32_t-based limit, which permits counts whose larger count * sizeof(*items) product wraps and underallocates the buffer the caller fills.
Items are uint64_t, so the retained SIZE_MAX / sizeof(uint64_t) limit checks the same product as the removed guard at [1].
Oversized counts still return before multiplication, preserving the required allocation-overflow protection.
The no-op at [2] replaces the element-width guard at [1].
The surviving uint32_t limit allows larger counts than uint64_t elements can safely occupy, letting the size product wrap before allocation despite the overflow rule.
Replacing [1] with the no-op at [2] leaves the uint64_t-based count limit in place.
Since items points to uint64_t, that remaining guard still rejects overflowing products before bytes is calculated and allocated.
